\section{Uncertainty Targets in the Recent Literature}
The following distinctions guide baseline selection. They do not rank methods that solve different problems on one inappropriate score. The accompanying dated survey has 119 curated candidates across reconstruction, poses, heterogeneity, map validation, atomic ensembles and general inverse inference; its source manifest distinguishes retrieved material from targeted critical reading and inaccessible full text. This is a scoped critical survey rather than a claim to have exhaustively reviewed all cryo-EM applications. Versioned preprints are identified separately from published articles.

\paragraph{Additional local and atomic validation.} The recent Gold-standard local toolbox compares half-map phase and amplitude, with explicit independent-noise assumptions in its SNR derivation \citep{goldlocal2026}. EMMIVox combines molecular force fields, map likelihoods and half-map-informed uncertainty for atomic refinement \citep{emmivox2024}. Neither output is the fixed raw-particle density functional studied here.

\paragraph{Distributional inverse stability.} The recent revision of
\citet{stochastic2026} separates image-distribution discrepancy from latent
Wasserstein error under assumed local stability. Its observability inequality
bounds stability above, not below; it does not certify experimental coverage.
A correctly specified Gaussian-mixture baseline wins its matched synthetic
comparison, illustrating the importance of retaining favorable baselines.

\paragraph{Direct statistical uncertainty prior art.} The probabilistic Fourier-slice model of \citet{ullrich2020} is a close reconstruction-uncertainty comparator and explicitly recognizes model bias. Joint likelihood soft modes \citep{rangan2024} expose pose--density ambiguities. \citet{lai2023} connect empirical Bayes and sequential MCMC filtering to dynamic image reconstruction, including scalar confidence sets and hybrid resampling. Their approximate fitted-family resampling and posterior computations differ from the present uniform conditional bounded-class statement; they cannot be dismissed as deterministic reconstruction methods. Neither general bias-aware inference nor the distinction between posterior variance and model error originates here.

\paragraph{Latent orientations and moment validation.}
Nonuniform moment recovery has explicit bandlimit and genericity conditions;
numerical Jacobian ranks in unknown-law cases differ from exact uniqueness
proofs \citep{sharon2020}. SubspaceMoM compresses moments to jointly recover
structure and viewing laws, with its principal reconstruction tests on
synthetic CTF-corrupted images \citep{subspacemom2026}.
High-noise Fisher stratification for marginalized orbit likelihoods assumes
Haar rotations, generic signals and projected identifiability conditions
\citep{fan2024}; it is not per-particle pose calibration.
Moment-based structural comparison also profiles a viewing-law expansion
\citep{momentmetrics2024}. Its 10076 example uses separate states and deposited
shifts, with remaining acquisition effects and limited close-state discrimination.
These are substantive alternatives to conditional local-pose analysis, without
establishing the same finite-sample feature guarantee.

Adjacent radiative CT work also separates analytic Gaussian uncertainty from shared reconstruction error and distinguishes foreground evaluation from whole-volume scores \citep{zhao2026radiative}. Its density-moment formulas and validation distinctions further constrain novelty claims; its acquisition and estimands differ from cryo-EM.

Bayes' Rays uses post-hoc displacement uncertainty for a frozen NeRF, with a diagonal curvature approximation \citep{goli2024}. Its spatial target differs from an additive density interval. The dynamic extension proposed in \citet[Section 5.2]{patel2025thesis} is explicitly future work, with cryo-EM as an intended application; we do not treat that proposal as an experimentally validated density guarantee.

\paragraph{Pose inference versus pose confidence.} Posterior-averaged orientation estimation \citep{bayespose2026} and probabilistic orientation search in SIMPLE \citep{simple2025} improve pose estimation through different statistical or optimization constructions. Neither an orientation distribution nor a stochastic search neighborhood should be relabeled a calibrated per-particle confidence ball without verifying its guarantee. Our prescribed local balls avoid that claim, but consequently do not solve practical pose calibration.

Cryo-forum uses quaternion-distribution dispersion for error ranking and filtering \citep{cryoforum2023}. ARCHER learns reference-conditioned pose scores and evaluates cross-specimen transfer and junk rejection \citep{archer2026}. CESPED standardizes experimental poses obtained by refinement, and explicitly acknowledges uncertainty in those labels \citep{cesped2024}. CryoPARES transfers alignments between related experiments \citep{cryopares2026}; CryoFastAR combines multiview pose prediction, synthetic training and experimental fine-tuning \citep{cryofastar2025}. These approaches address efficiency and different transfer settings. Their quality scores and angular errors cannot supply a uniform maximum-error radius for every particle in a new stack. The $0.1^\circ$ and $0.5^\circ$ budgets in our frozen study are sensitivity settings, not experimentally established alignment accuracy.

\paragraph{Physical heterogeneity versus estimation error.} RECOVAR estimates covariance and uses kernel regression to account for noisy latent coordinates \citep{recovar2025}. DynaMight and 3DFlex represent motion \citep{dynamight2024,flex2023}. Particle-counting work explicitly studies when assignments misestimate state populations \citep{counting2026}. These motivate separate tests of population recovery, structural variation and uncertainty in a homogeneous density. The present bounded-density target covers only the last. CryoDRGN-AI addresses joint ab initio reconstruction \citep{drgnai2025}; fixed-pose homogeneous training does not reproduce that task.

DynaMight's held-out deformation disagreement and independent-half training assess motion errors; 3DFlex separates lower-frequency motion training from higher-frequency reconstruction validation. Their protocols must be examined at the level of shared components and evaluated frequencies. \citet{mattingly2026} study how the image model limits learnable conformational populations, using information-based selection of ensemble granularity. That prior-averaged population target differs from our fixed homogeneous density functional. CryoBench likewise distinguishes representation learning, conformation assignment and volume recovery with several reference-based FSC metrics \citep{cryobench2025}. Our simulations posit one density per acquisition geometry; the actual stacks need not be homogeneous. In particular, the assembly-intermediate mixture in EMPIAR-10076 does not validate our shared-density assumption.

\paragraph{Map validation and learned priors.} False-discovery confidence maps test density significance against a noise reference \citep{beckers2019}. Directional resolution measures acquisition anisotropy \citep{monodir2020}; independent-particle tests assess map fit \citep{independent2020}. Bias/variance analyses explain why validation requires more than internal agreement \citep{sorzano2022}. Blush introduces learned reconstruction regularization \citep{blush2024}, while LocScale-2.0 attaches confidence to enhancement relative to its stated proxy \citep{locscale2026}. Compressed-image recovery with cryoSENSE targets acquisition fidelity rather than density-confidence coverage \citep{cryosense2026}. Matched evaluations must retain these targets. A sharper-looking map or a significant positive voxel is not itself a bound on error relative to unknown density.

Fixed-candidate ensemble analysis also separates discretization bias, statistical variability and early stopping \citep{mordant2026}. Its simplified known-likelihood population problem differs from spatial density reconstruction with uncertain poses; it does not calibrate the nuisance bounds used here.

CryoRes predicts local resolution using deposited and algorithm-derived training labels \citep{cryores2023}. Such supervision inherits the meaning of those labels; it does not transform a resolution score into a confidence interval. Similarly, held-out image prediction measures agreement with new observations, and can remain favorable when two reconstructions share unsupported density directions. Ground-truth simulation, new-exposure prediction, directional diagnostics and independent structural evidence therefore complement one another.

\paragraph{Invariant compression and thermodynamic targets.} Moment-based posterior sampling conditions a learned prior on shift-invariant power spectra in one-dimensional orbit recovery \citep{janson2025}. Compression discards phase information, so posterior concentration can rely on the prior. Separately, cryoTWIN/PaStEL targets conformational free energies under sampling, pose and equilibrium assumptions \citep{cryotwin2026}. Neither problem is equivalent to our shared-density feature interval.

\paragraph{Atomic ensembles and independent modalities.} Experiment-guided AlphaFold3 conditions structural generation on reconstructed ESP maps and other measurements \citep{guidedaf32026}. Its atomic-ensemble target differs from raw-particle density inference. The multimodal examples also illustrate why improved map agreement need not imply improved fit to a separate measurement modality. Independent evidence is relevant to assessing structural interpretations that the density measurements alone leave ambiguous.

\paragraph{Coordinate-error conformal prediction.} CalPro calibrates protein-coordinate error scores at an exchangeable-protein level \citep{calpro2026}. Its atomic target and calibration unit differ from a fixed density feature inferred from noisy projections. We do not interpret a calibrated protein-average score as simultaneous residue coverage or as experimental-density coverage.

\paragraph{Simultaneous inverse inference.} Constrained test-inversion methods already address joint confidence regions for multiple functionals \citep{batlle2025}. A single data-consistency region can support simultaneous projections, whereas separately calibrated marginal intervals generally require an appropriate correction. Our present scalar-target theorem is not a new general framework for simultaneous inference, and a colored map of marginal intervals must not be presented as simultaneous coverage.

\paragraph{Conformal calibration and its sampling unit.} Posterior-variance calibration can provide error bounds even when a posterior sampler is approximate \citep{narnhofer2024}; its theorem uses independent identically distributed signal--observation pairs and conditions on a variance bin. QUTCC learns quantile-dependent image predictions and calibrates marginal pixel errors from paired reference images \citep{qutcc2026}. These methods can be useful without our fixed-signal radius assumption, but require a calibration population with the stated sampling relationship to deployment. Voxels or noise draws from one molecule are not automatically independent calibration molecules. Neither marginal population coverage nor variance-bin coverage is the same as coverage uniformly over every density in a specified class.

\paragraph{Prior-assisted alignment and atomic refinement.} CryoPROS uses generated auxiliary particles for pose correction, with template-variation and noise-only controls \citep{cryopros2025}. Such tests address model bias without calibrating experimental pose confidence regions. CoCoFold fine-tunes AlphaFold against particle images using a Gaussian-mixture forward model and supplied poses/CTFs \citep{cocofold2026}. Its pose-perturbation checks support a sensitivity comparison, not a density-coverage guarantee. Both motivate independent validation of prior-assisted inference; neither is a matched density-functional uncertainty baseline here.

\paragraph{Open questions suggested by the survey.} Particularly consequential gaps are absolute pose-confidence calibration under reference error; uncertainty in conformational populations when candidate structures are imperfect; validation of detail introduced by learned priors using independent particles; and uncertainty propagation through CTF fitting, image preprocessing, alignment and atomic interpretation. Acquisition chosen for a specific structural feature is another possible application of adjoint sensitivity. These are directions inferred from the literature, not priority claims or completed capabilities of this implementation. The present continuous audit addresses representation exclusion under stated nuisance assumptions; solving those assumptions empirically remains distinct work.

\subsection{Experimental reconstruction and prediction context}
We execute stock cryoDRGN 4.3.1 homogeneous neural training on both exposure-group halves of all three stacks: three hidden layers, width 256, batch size eight, fixed consensus poses and CTFs. These are actual neural fits; they are not ab initio inference or uncertainty estimates. Gaussian and voxel ridge fits use the same halves. All methods are evaluated on identical held-out particles and 1,410 Fourier pairs per image inside radius 30 of the 64-pixel grid, with the same window and image-background normalization. Neural training itself uses the stock radius-32 loss and per-half global scaling, so training objectives are not identical.

Table~\ref{tab:reconstruction} selects checkpoints using tuning-group error only, from runs through 60 epochs for EMPIAR-10028/10049 and 100 epochs for EMPIAR-10076. The selected epochs are 60, 50 and 100. Two are the last available checkpoints, so undertraining remains possible. The development plateau check motivated these budgets; it is not a preregistered stopping rule or a proof of global convergence. Exposure-group bootstrap comparisons, checkpoint hashes and direct-network versus map-Fourier checks are recorded with the results. FSC assesses conditional map agreement; neither it nor image prediction labels true experimental density coverage.
\input{uncertainty-reconstruction-results.tex}

A frozen follow-up evaluates these unchanged models on 4,096 additional particles per dataset from exposure groups absent from development (Table~\ref{tab:freshprediction}). Neural prediction has lower NMSE than both controls in all three datasets; all six prespecified paired group-bootstrap differences remain positive under the stated multiplicity adjustment. This confirms conditional prediction ranking on new exposures, not experimental density coverage or independent-pose FSC.

Post-hoc background diagnostics on all 12,288 new images show mean nearest-neighbor normalized pair products of 0.197--0.292 across the three stacks and two image axes (Figure~\ref{fig:background}). White-Gaussian controls with the same background centering and normalization are near zero. The annular background can contain molecular signal, ice and preprocessing artifacts, so this is not identification of the measurement-noise law. It does show why simple spatial scaling cannot be assumed to establish whitening; our supplied-noise simulations do not resolve that experimental issue.

Table~\ref{tab:ambient} reports median widths across the two targets. The full-space solver reached its 0.5\% objective-gap tolerance in 12 of 12 cases, taking 2.4--11.1 seconds per target on the Mac. The enrichment solver reached the same outer tolerance in 8 of 12 cases within 100 rounds; nonconverged results retain valid bounds but do not establish optimality. The solvers optimize the conservative sum-width, so their sharper reported widths need not be ordered exactly by their objective gaps.

Dictionary-only intervals can be narrow because they exclude admissible density errors. For the EMPIAR-10028 central broad average, analytic coverage on the independent voxel-map generator is approximately $4.2\times10^{-5}$. The same image weights, with the ambient bias bound, cover at the prescribed level over the ambient ball. On each estimator's constructed ambient bias boundary, the audited intervals attain nominal 0.95 Gaussian coverage up to numerical tolerance. These boundary calculations check the theorem and implementation; they are not independent evidence of practical class calibration. Broader targets have substantially smaller relative widths than fine targets. The prescribed norm radius and fixed-pose assumption are essential to interpreting that result.

\section{Development After Independent Review}\label{sec:revision}
The original frozen protocols and their outcomes are unchanged. This section
reports subsequent development, including negative experimental sensitivity
results. It does not establish that the current method meets the usefulness
requirements raised by the independent review.
The old frozen evaluators abort on detected undercoverage before retaining the
offending record. Neither completed study encountered that branch, but the
failure policy was flawed. Their source remains reproducible; new diagnostic
evaluators persist results before flagging an audit failure.

\subsection{Matrix-free shared fields and a numerical failure budget}
Each first or second pose-derivative field is a Fourier sum multiplied by one of
ten monomials $1,x,y,z,x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,xz,yz$. Summing coefficient combinations
before transforming gives a field/adjoint pair with ten type-3 NUFFTs per
direction. No global particle-by-particle field Gram is formed. Positive group
scales $d_j$ may come from streamed block norms or from polynomial coefficient
envelopes. They need not equal exact block norms. Identically zero blocks may
be omitted; blocks that can become nonzero during optimization require positive
scales. Particle-specific pose radii are accepted.

An approximate leading eigenvalue is insufficient for an upper audit. Random
starts have a long history in spectral estimation \citep{kw1992}; the following
elementary construction states our particular numerical probability budget.
For a fixed positive semidefinite $C=FF^\top$, draw $m$ independent standard
Gaussian probes $g_j$, independently of the estimator-selection process. Set
$c=\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(\delta^{1/m})$. Fix a leading unit
eigenvector $v$ before the draws. Since
\[
 \Pr\{\max_j|v^\top g_j|<c\}=\delta,
\]
with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every integer $p\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_{\max}(C)
 \le \left(\frac{\max_j\norm{C^p g_j}}{c}\right)^{1/p}.
 \label{eq:randompower}
\end{equation}
The proof retains the leading eigenvector component of $C^p g_j$ in its norm.
Stable normalization tracks the product of norms in log space. The minimum
across powers is valid on the same event; a deterministic trace bound may cap
it. A Rayleigh value is recorded only as a lower diagnostic.

Add the analytic integration pad to this spectral upper value before using the
shared-field inequality. Allocate $\alpha_{\rm noise}+\delta\le\alpha$. A union
bound then includes numerical randomization in the stated failure budget.
Candidate selection using the same probes is not licensed: weights and scales
must be fixed before fresh final probes, or all candidates need a simultaneous
budget. Operator roundoff and NUFFT approximation remain numerical checks,
not validated arithmetic.

Completed radius-five audits with 128 and 1,024 particles take 50.3 and 353.3
seconds under concurrent Mac load, with measured peak resident memory of 390
and 434 MB. Their relative half-widths are 0.438 and 0.740, respectively. They
use different fitted estimators, so the latter result does not measure a
particle-count benefit. The 128-particle randomized field bound is 1.157 times
the dense comparator. A distinct 10,000-particle, radius-12 audit with 220
independent Fourier pairs per particle completes in 4,965 seconds with 1.95 GB
peak resident memory. Its randomized eigenvalue upper is 1.136 times the
Rayleigh lower diagnostic. Relative half-width is 0.655 at $1^\circ$ and
0.5\,\AA\ translation. This uses deterministic matched-filter weights for a
broad target, not optimized reconstruction weights. It establishes numerical
scale under supplied simulation bounds, not useful fine-feature inference.

\subsection{Including pose uncertainty in estimator optimization}
Fix the group scales, let $F(w)$ be the scaled quadrature field matrix, and let
$a_q(w)$ be each real/imaginary weight pair's Euclidean amplitude. A nonnegative
matrix $M$ maps these amplitudes to polynomial coefficient envelopes. With
integration constant $E$, $R=B+P$, and integrated cubic coefficients $r_q\ge0$,
the revised sum objective is
\begin{align}
 J(w)&=z\norm{w}+B\norm{\ell-\A^*w}+p(w)
       +\sum_q r_q a_q(w),\nonumber\\
 p(w)&=R\sqrt{\sum_jd_j}
 \sqrt{\norm{F(w)}_{\rm op}^2+E\norm{Ma(w)}^2}.
 \label{eq:poseoptimized}
\end{align}
This is convex: $F$ is linear, $M$ is nonnegative, and the Euclidean norm is
monotone on the nonnegative orthant. It is an upper objective for the prescribed
class, not the exact minimax nonlinear-pose risk. Approximate singular modes
and log-sum-exp smoothing guide numerical optimization. The final primal upper
audit uses Equation~\eqref{eq:randompower} with fresh probes.

A feasible dual lower bound remains available without an optimizer-success
claim. Choose $v\in H$ and supporting linear functionals $g_p,g_r$ such that
\begin{align*}
 \norm{v}&\le B,&\norm{\A v-g_p-g_r}&\le z,\\
 g_p^\top x&\le p(x),&
 g_r^\top x&\le\sum_qr_q a_q(x)\quad\text{for all }x.
\end{align*}
The four support inequalities in Equation~\eqref{eq:poseoptimized} yield
$J(x)\ge\ip{v}{\ell}$ by cancellation. Unit singular-direction outer products
and their convex mixtures have nuclear norm at most one, giving valid spectral
supports even when the selected modes are not leading. Coefficient and cubic
norm supports are combined with them. A padded continuous Gram-action error
bounds the remaining dual constraint; scaling all three dual quantities by
$\min(1,z/D)$ for an upper bound $D$ makes it feasible. The implementation
details and full support argument are recorded with the source.

An independently assembled small CLARABEL conic instance brackets its optimum
with relative gap $2.60\times10^{-4}$. The first larger, 20-iteration development
solve reduces a one-degree interval to 0.255 of no data but has a 97.8\% gap;
it is not converged. Six subsequent feasible nonlinear searches reach 0.432 of
its bias upper bound, and minimum reference sign power is below $10^{-100}$.
The first completed 100-iteration case in the three-stack grid, 10049 at
$0.5^\circ$ and 0.5\,\AA\ translation, has relative width 0.221 and a 25.3\%
gap. Feasible searches reach 0.608 of its bias upper, but minimum reference
sign power is only $8.44\times10^{-5}$. Its completed one-degree counterpart
has width 0.336, an 85.3\% gap and minimum reference power $7.07\times10^{-25}$.
A feasible convex mixture of twelve spectral dual supports reduces the gap
only to 85.1\%, without changing the estimator or interval.

The original 10028 half-degree run failed when only seven of eight requested
eigenvectors converged; the failure and saved weights are retained. Checkpointed
continuations use an isolated two-thread CPU runtime with unchanged block
scales and fresh final spectral probes. Available partial modes can guide the
approximate optimizer, but are never used as upper bounds. The completed
10076 half-degree continuation has width 0.161, a 5.0\% gap, minimum reference
sign power 0.670, and feasible stress bias reaching 0.650 of the upper bound.
The full eighteen-case grid (three stacks, two broad targets and
$0.5^\circ,1^\circ,2^\circ$ with 0.5\,\AA\ shifts) is now complete,
including nonconverged fits. After the declared sharper remainder and known-pilot
pairing, all six two-degree relative widths are 0.427--0.633, feasible-bias/upper
ratios are 0.274--0.360, and the largest minimum-reference sign power is
$3.27\times10^{-72}$. Thus the grid does not meet the requested all-stack
width, bound-tightness or useful-detection criterion. The final 10028 contrast
case has a 99.8\% original sum-objective gap and a refined width 0.514;
completion does not establish optimization convergence. Table~\ref{tab:joint-bias}
also retains three separately declared 10049 follow-up optimizations.

\paragraph{Nonsmooth optimization and dual diagnostics.}
The longer legacy one-degree smooth probe fails before its final audit when
only seven of eight modes converge; it has no certified result. To separate
optimizer failure from estimator quality, we also restrict weights to $w=Vb$
and exchange spectral supporting cuts. For unit $u,v$,
$g^\top w=v^\top F(w)u\le\norm{F(w)}_{\rm op}$.
Noise, density-residual and cubic pair norms then form a small conic problem
with constraints $t\ge g_j^\top Vb$. The unknown density class remains
continuous. The restricted cut value is an optimization device, not a
full-space lower bound; integration padding and fresh spectral probes remain
in the final audit.

Conic cut multipliers obey $\mu_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\mu_j\le
R\sqrt{\sum d}$, so $\sum_j\mu_jg_j$ is a valid full-space pose dual
support. Cubic cone duals, projected onto their known pair balls, avoid
normalizing nearly zero weight pairs. More generally, minimizing the dual
constraint defect over a convex hull of pose supports plus these pair balls
can improve a lower bound without changing any interval. An independent
small full spectral-norm conic problem checks the cut solver and support
inequalities, including a nonzero optimum and an active zero pair.

On 10049 at two degrees and 0.5\,\AA, the original completed fit has relative
width 0.761 and a 99.3\% gap. Joint dual postprocessing reduces that gap to
63.1\% with unchanged weights. Two consecutive thirty-round restricted-cut
probes reduce width to 0.692 and 0.689. Their final local feasible stress
biases reach 0.459 and 0.466 of the respective upper bounds; reference sign
power remains below $10^{-240}$. The follow-up's own joint dual gap is still
93.9\%. These limited subspaces and dual directions do not establish full-space
optimality or useful detection at two degrees.

A six-round conic trial optimizes all observation weights, projecting only
the inner density residual onto a target-anchored continuous Hilbert basis.
The projected residual is a lower relaxation, while the final audit retains
the full density class. At rank 256 the new candidates have much larger
ambient objectives than the input; the retained weights are unchanged.
A fresh audit gives width 0.690 and gap 76.2\%. A thirty-round adaptive
continuous residual-enrichment follow-up takes 721 seconds and raises the
valid lower bound to 9.200, reducing the original sum-objective gap to
18.2\%, again with unchanged weights. This gap concerns the original triangle
objective, not the subsequent tighter cross-term bound. These diagnostics
distinguish improved lower bounds from an improved reconstruction.

A sixty-round full-weight continuation, with the latest eight candidates
averaged before independent evaluation, changes the retained weights. It takes
2,330 seconds, gives a sum-objective upper bound 10.523 and feasible lower
bound 9.845 (6.44\% gap), and reduces the relative width to 0.646. The
strongest saved feasible nonlinear bias reaches 0.521 of its upper bound.
This establishes progress on the original objective, not useful reference
sign detection or optimality of the subsequent joint expression.

A further sixty rounds use the sharp cubic constants and therefore reset
the lower bound for the changed objective. They take 4,666 seconds and give
upper/lower values 9.8961/9.5935 (3.06\% gap), with relative width 0.607.
The subsequent cross-term and known-pilot audits reduce that width to 0.548
and 0.503, respectively. The strongest saved nonlinear bias is 0.630 of the
last upper, but minimum reference sign power remains below $10^{-118}$.
Those later widths do not inherit the sum-objective optimization gap.

\paragraph{Retaining the density/pose cross term.}
Let $h=\ell-A_0^*w$ and write the existing nonlinear adjoint perturbation as
$D=Fv+e$, where $\norm v\le L=\sqrt{\sum d}$ and $\norm e\le r$.
Here each particle lies in the joint scaled five-dimensional unit ball.
Simultaneous maximal rotation and translation are excluded. For their product
set, replace $L^2$ by $2\sum_i d_i^{(1)}+4\sum_i d_i^{(2)}$ and scale $f$
by the corresponding radius ratio. The separate phase bounds in the cubic
remainder already cover either set. The two nuisance classes are reported
separately.
Suppose $f$ bounds $\norm{Fv}$ and $c$ bounds $\norm{F^*h}$.
The scalar bias for $\rho=\rho_0+u$ is
$\langle u,h-D\rangle-\langle\rho_0,D\rangle$. Thus
\begin{equation}
 b_{\rm joint}=B\sqrt{\norm h^2+2Lc+f^2}+Pf+(B+P)r
 \label{eq:joint-cross-bias}
\end{equation}
is an upper bound: expand $\norm{h-Fv}^2$, bound the cross term by $Lc$,
and apply Cauchy--Schwarz to $u$ and $\rho_0$. Take the minimum with the
preceding triangle bound on the same spectral event. This elementary
inequality is a post-audit refinement, not a new general theorem or a
claim that the expression is convex in $w$.

Gaussian target moments evaluate $\langle\ell,F_j\rangle$ analytically
on the cube, including boundary terms. For
$I_j=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}x^jg_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}\,dx$,
integration by parts gives
\begin{align*}
 I_1&=(\mu+is^2\omega)I_0-s^2[g_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}]_{-1/2}^{1/2},\\
 I_2&=(\mu+is^2\omega)I_1+s^2I_0
       -s^2[xg_{\mu,s}(x)e^{i\omega x}]_{-1/2}^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
For the finite Fourier-polynomial product $\langle A_0^*w,F_j\rangle$,
the existing quadrature error gives a cross-vector norm pad $ET\norm m$,
where $T$ is the absolute Fourier coefficient sum and $m$ contains the
scaled column coefficient bounds. Ordinary numerical roundoff remains
subject to the preceding caveat.

Table~\ref{tab:joint-bias} retains the completed same-weight audits at
this revision cutoff; the machine-readable summary lists every attempt and
its source certificate seed. Each row uses its own source spectral event,
without selecting a minimum over repeated random certificates.
The 10076 half-degree conditional reference power increases from 0.670
to 0.968; the two-degree cut fit improves from width 0.689 to 0.598,
but its reference power remains negligible. The saved nonlinear feasible
stresses do not violate any new bound. This is evidence of reduced
conservatism on these cases, not experimental density coverage.
\input{tables/joint-bias}

An optional further constant refinement uses the sharp cube directional
moments $\sup_{\norm u=1}\mathbb{E}(u^\top X)^4=13/720$ and
$\sup_{\norm u=1}\mathbb{E}(u^\top X)^6=205/36288$, for uniform cube $X$.
Writing $p_j=u_j^2$, the sixth moment is
$5/576-\sum p_j^2/96+\sum p_j^3/252$; pairwise averaging maximizes it
at $p_j=1/3$. Replacing the earlier Gaussian moment majorants in the same
integrated remainder reduces the two-degree cut-fit width further to 0.572.
For the full-weight averaged fit, the joint and sharp-moment refinements give
widths 0.581 and 0.557, with feasible-over-upper ratios 0.582 and 0.608.
Expanding to the product pose set increases the latter width to 0.616; saved
joint-ball adversaries remain feasible examples but do not explore its extra
poses. Minimum reference sign power remains below $10^{-155}$ even for the
sharp joint-ball result. Independent tests exercise archive-scale Gaussian
moments, the analytic cross-product quadrature pad, and the distinction
between joint and product pose lifts. The original fit and every previous
bound are retained. Neither refinement establishes useful fine-feature
detection at one or two degrees.

\paragraph{Using the known pilot.}
The pilot term need not pay its full norm bound. If
$p\ge\norm{F^*\rho_0}$, Cauchy--Schwarz also gives
$|\langle\rho_0,Fv\rangle|\le Lp$. Hence the same spectral event supports
\begin{equation}
 b_{\rm pilot}=B\sqrt{\norm h^2+2Lc+f^2}
       +\min(Pf,Lp)+(B+P)r.
 \label{eq:pilot-cross-bias}
\end{equation}
The triangle alternative replaces the square root by $\norm h+f$;
their minimum remains valid. This changes neither the unknown density class
nor the weights. It is an elementary refinement of the known-function term,
not a new general coverage theorem or an optimization-gap certificate.

For the known orthonormal constant-cell pilot on an $m^3$ grid, write
$x=c+z$ inside each cell. For a uniform offset
$z\in[-1/(2m),1/(2m)]$, with $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E e^{2\pi i k z}&=\operatorname{sinc}(k/m),\\
 \mathbb E z e^{2\pi i k z}&=\frac{\operatorname{sinc}'(k/m)}{2\pi i m},\\
 \mathbb E z^2 e^{2\pi i k z}&=-\frac{\operatorname{sinc}''(k/m)}{4\pi^2m^2}.
\end{align*}
Expanding $x^\beta=(c+z)^\beta$ gives all ten degree-at-most-two
Fourier moments from ten transforms of center-weighted cell coefficients.
The orthonormal basis supplies $m^{-3/2}$ and the centered Fourier grid
requires phase $\exp(i\pi\sum_a k_a/m)$. Thus the known discontinuous
pilot is integrated over its cells, without replacing the unknown density
by a cell representation. Near zero we evaluate the sinc derivatives by
their Taylor series.

Independent composite cell quadrature and nonlinear finite differences
check normalization and pose signs. Direct exponential sums over the actual
$24^3$ centers check all twenty lifted columns for three selected particles
in each of the first ten archived audits. The largest relative pairing
discrepancy is $3.49\times10^{-13}$; this selected-column check is not a
global floating-point error bound. The analytic formula has no quadrature
error, but its NUFFT and floating-point evaluation remain numerically
checked rather than interval-validated.

Table~\ref{tab:pilot-pairing} reports this separate same-weight variant.
For the full-weight two-degree fit, the width falls from 0.557 to 0.510,
and the saved feasible-over-upper ratio rises to 0.667. Its minimum
reference sign power is still below $5\times10^{-122}$. The 10076 broad
central feature has power 0.997 at half a degree and 0.214 at one degree;
its two-degree width is 0.427, with negligible power. These conditional
improvements leave fine-scale usefulness and experimental calibration open.

\subsection{An experimental noise-calibration attempt}
The following elementary conservative calculation allows nonzero calibration
signals. Suppose independent $Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\Sigma)$ have arbitrary fixed
means and a common covariance. Put $T=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$ and
$S=\sum_i\norm{Y_i}^2$. For $\lambda>0$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E e^{-\lambda S}
 &\le\det(I+2\lambda\Sigma)^{-n/2}\\
 &\le(1+2\lambda T)^{-n/2}.
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from the noncentral Gaussian Laplace transform;
the second uses $\prod_j(1+x_j)\ge1+\sum_jx_j$ for nonnegative eigenvalues.
Optimizing the exponential Markov inequality gives
\[
 \Pr\{S\le ntT\}\le
 \exp\{n(1-t+\log t)/2\},\qquad 0<t<1.
\]
Choose $t$ to make the right side $\beta$. Then $T_+=S/(nt)$ is an upper bound
on $T$ with probability at least $1-\beta$, and $\Sigma\preceq T_+I$ on that
event. This can be much more conservative than estimating a known diagonal
noise model. Independent inference with the same covariance permits allocating
$\alpha_{\rm noise}+\beta\le\alpha$. The result does not prove the covariance
commonality or pose-independence assumptions for archive data.

The exploratory three-stack attempt fits each old pilot's scalar amplitude on
pilot-pool particles, then calibrates from one particle per new exposure group.
Half of the new groups calibrate, and the others supply energy diagnostics.
Inference also uses one particle per old inference exposure group. No background
mask or fitted-signal subtraction enters the calibration statistic. We use
$\beta=0.005$, $\alpha_{\rm noise}=0.045$, density radius two, and prescribed
0/1/2-degree sensitivities with 0.5\,\AA\ shifts at nonzero angles.

All eighteen intervals contain their amplitude-aligned deposited-map value;
none excludes zero. This is a precision failure, not evidence of density
calibration. The 10\,\AA\ targets revert to no data at nonzero pose budgets.
The earlier 128-particle attempt on 10028 is also retained; it additionally
requires unverified independence within repeated exposure groups.

\paragraph{Independent calibration in the estimator's directions.}
The trace envelope protects every direction, although a fixed feature estimator
needs only one scalar variance. Let $V$ contain its raw-coordinate particle
weight rows $v_i^\top$, chosen independently of a second calibration pool.
Under the same common-covariance and independence assumptions, its noise
variance is $s^2=\sum_i v_i^\top\Sigma v_i=\operatorname{tr}(V\Sigma V^\top)$.
Applying the preceding lemma to $VY_j$ gives the following direct corollary:
\[
 s^2\le s_+^2:=\frac{\sum_j\norm{VY_j}^2}{nt}
 \quad\text{with probability at least }1-\beta.
\]
The projected coordinates may be correlated. Combining this event with the
bias-aware critical width at $\alpha_{\rm noise}$ gives pointwise failure at
most $\beta+\alpha_{\rm noise}$. Indeed, the width is at least the bias bound,
and its Gaussian outside probability increases with noise scale. This is an
elementary specialization of the trace argument, not a new concentration
principle or a simultaneous guarantee for selected targets.

For the same calibration pool, $\sum_j\norm{VY_j}^2\le
\norm{V}_F^2\sum_j\norm{Y_j}^2$, so directional calibration cannot exceed
the original trace envelope for these weights. To preserve independence here,
we retain weights selected using the original first exposure half and calibrate
their variance with the second half. The pools therefore differ in the empirical
comparison. Before projection, weights are pulled back through each particle's
known centering phase: complex coefficient $w_R+iw_I$ becomes
$\overline p(w_R+iw_I)/\sigma_{\rm old}$ in raw Fourier coordinates.
Ignoring this step would be incorrect for colored noise.

\input{tables/directional-noise}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering\includegraphics[width=.98\textwidth]{figures/directional-noise.pdf}
\caption{All eighteen experimental directional-noise sensitivity cases.
Only the calibration bound changes; weights and continuous bias terms are
held fixed. The single interval excluding zero is the broad 10076 target at
fixed pose; it does not exclude zero at one degree. Noise, density and pose
assumptions remain unverified, and the previously inspected diagnostic pool
makes this exploratory reuse rather than a new frozen confirmation.}
\label{fig:directionalnoise}
\end{figure*}

The new standard-deviation bounds are 0.132--0.285 times the original bounds.
One broad fixed-pose interval excludes zero; none does at one or two degrees.
Thus reducing this avoidable noise conservatism does not resolve the
pose/density precision problem. No experimental density-coverage inference
follows from deposited-map agreement or this conditional fixed-pose detection.

\paragraph{Repeated particles within an inference exposure.}
The calibration can retain one independent representative per calibration
exposure while allowing arbitrary jointly Gaussian dependence among inference
particles from the same exposure. If exposure $g$ has $n_g$ particles and
$X_i=v_i^\top\epsilon_i$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in g}X_i\right)
 \le\left(\sum_{i\in g}\sqrt{v_i^\top\Sigma v_i}\right)^2
 \le n_g\sum_{i\in g}v_i^\top\Sigma v_i.
\]
Thus replace row $v_i$ of $V$ by $\sqrt{n_g}v_i$ in the trace calibration.
This elementary extension removes within-exposure independence; it retains
between-exposure independence, a common marginal raw covariance, Gaussianity,
and independence of the weights and supplied design from the relevant noise.
It does not establish those conditions for the archive particles.

\paragraph{Refitting with an independent covariance guide.}
We also use the first exposure half's uncentered second moment $\widehat C$
to form $C=0.8\widehat C+0.2\operatorname{tr}(\widehat C)I/m$; the second half
still supplies the final directional noise bound. This positive matrix guides
optimization only. With known centering matrices $O_i$, set
$W=\operatorname{diag}_i[(O_iCO_i^\top)^{-1/2}]$ and write $w=Wx$.
The continuous fixed-pose problem then uses target vector $W\A\ell$ and Gram
$WGW$. Its proxy objective is $z\norm{x}+B\norm{\ell-\A^*Wx}$.
Quadrature residual errors are evaluated at $Wx$; transformed Gram-action
errors multiply by $\norm W$. None of these proxy quantities replaces the
independent final noise or pose audit.

\input{tables/noise-metric-design}
All six proxy fits reach a sum-objective gap below 0.33\%. Their fixed-pose
intervals improve, but five one-degree intervals widen and the sixth remains
vacuous. Nine of eighteen settings now use no data, including every two-degree
setting. Only the same broad 10076 fixed-pose interval excludes zero. Thus
better noise-guided fixed-pose fitting can amplify pose sensitivity; it does
not substitute for joint pose-aware design.

\paragraph{A larger physical 10\,\AA\ target.}
On 1,024 particles from 10049 at Fourier radius 12, with target Gaussian
standard deviation $10\,\AA$ and sampled band ending at $19.68\,\AA$, an order-80 continuous
fixed-pose fit reaches sum-objective gap 0.000992 in 3,583 seconds, with
relative half-width 0.01378. The independent normalized reference-map central
value is 1.9245; conditional sign power is one at fixed pose. Keeping those
weights and auditing a joint ball of one degree and $0.5\,\AA$ changes the
conclusion: even with sharp cube constants, residual cross terms and the
known-pilot refinement, the result uses the no-data interval and has zero
sign power. The polynomial pose term is 6.376 and the cubic remainder is
56.493; the final unselected half-width is 61.223, exceeding the no-data
half-width 34.390. The pose audit takes 1,491 seconds and 1.08 GB peak
resident memory. Thus increasing the particle count and band does not by
itself control the nonlinear remainder. These are conditional development
results under supplied noise and nuisance bounds; the 128- and 1,024-particle
subsets are not nested, and the latter fit is not pose-optimized.

\input{enclosing-domain}

\subsection{Uniform CTF sensitivities}
For fixed voltage, spherical aberration and amplitude contrast $a$,
$C=\sin(\gamma-\arcsin a)$. If each defocus axis can change by $d$ and its
astigmatism angle by $b$ radians, a conservative defocus error is
$d+|\mathrm{df}_U-\mathrm{df}_V|\sin(\min(b,\pi/2))$. Multiplying by
$\pi\lambda s^2$ and adding the phase-shift radius bounds the phase error.
Evaluate the exact sine range on that interval, then multiply by the positive
relative gain/B-factor range. This yields an absolute transfer envelope
$e_{iq}$ without division by a CTF zero.

For any allowed pose, a complex Fourier wave has unit modulus on the unit-volume
cube. Therefore the additive CTF bias is bounded by
\begin{equation}
 b_{\rm CTF}\le (B+P)\sum_{iq}
       |w_{iq,\mathbb C}|e_{iq}/\sigma.
\end{equation}
This term can be combined with the nominal-CTF pose bound, including simultaneous
errors, but discards cancellations and is not optimized jointly with them.
Table~\ref{tab:revisionctf} applies it to all six saved radius-12 fixed-pose
fine-feature fits. Defocus uncertainty of 100\,\AA\ already causes two no-data
fallbacks; all six fall back at 500\,\AA\ and under the combined sensitivities.
These negative results diagnose a loose audit, not an impossibility theorem for
other estimators or a calibrated distribution of experimental CTF error.
\input{tables/revision-ctf}

\subsection{An explicit support ablation}
Changing support changes the density class. For a centered cube of side
$s\le1$, the transformation $\widetilde\rho(u)=s^{3/2}\rho(su)$ is an $L^2$
isometry. The transformed acquisition uses $k'=sk$, $q'=sq$, $C'=s^{3/2}C$
and translation radius $t'=t/s$. A normalized Gaussian target uses center
$c/s$, width $\sigma_\ell/s$ and amplitude $s^{-3/2}$. Thus the target and
nonlinear acquisition values are preserved, including physical translations.

Hard support need not be imposed without a sensitivity allowance. Write
$\rho=p_S+d_S+r_{S^c}$, where $p_S,d_S$ are supported inside the smaller cube,
$\norm{d_S}\le B$ and $\norm{r_{S^c}}\le\epsilon$. Add to the inside audit
\begin{align}
 b_{\rm tail}&\le\epsilon\left[\norm{\A_0^*w-\ell}
               +\sum_{iq}|c_{iq}|d_{iq}\right],\nonumber\\
 d_{iq}&=\min\!\left(2,2\pi\sqrt{
    \theta^2\norm{k_{iq}}^2/12+t^2\norm{q_{iq}}^2}\right).
\end{align}
Indeed, the spatial phase has zero mean on the cube, its integrated squared
linear part is $\norm{\Delta k}^2/12$, and the rotation chord is at most
$\theta\norm{k}$. Apply $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le\min(2,|a-b|)$ and the triangle
inequality, then restrict the residual to $S^c$. The bound is conservative;
it does not infer $\epsilon$ from the data.

The initial radius-12, 10\,\AA\-sigma support probe on 10049 uses 128 particles,
$1^\circ$ and 0.5\,\AA\ translation. Side $s=0.5$ gives relative width 0.417
under hard support, yet the cropped-reference minimum sign power is below
$10^{-150}$. A tail radius of 0.1 causes no-data fallback. The original
unit-norm reference has outside norm 0.320 and is excluded by all these tail
settings; it is not relabeled as an in-class validation example. The completed
full-cube control takes 6,324 seconds, attains a fixed-pose sum-objective gap
of 0.19\%, and falls back to no data at every tested tail allowance after
adding pose sensitivity. Its integrated cubic term alone is 115.4 in the
normalized density units. A converged nominal fit therefore does not establish
a useful pose-aware interval.

\paragraph{Signs and a total-norm bound.}
A separate same-weight ablation uses the alternative class
$\mathcal C(R,\eta)=\{f:\norm f\le R,\norm{f_-}\le\eta\}$,
where $0\le\eta\le R$ and $f_-=\max(-f,0)$. This is a different
origin-centered class, not a substituted radius in the old pilot interval.
For $h=\ell-\A_0^*w$, put $a=\norm{h_+}$ and $b=\norm{h_-}$.
Its elementary support function is
\[
 S_\eta(h)=\begin{cases}
 R\sqrt{a^2+b^2},& Rb\le\eta\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\\
 \sqrt{R^2-\eta^2}\,a+\eta b,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The optimal positive/negative components align with $h_+$ and $h_-$;
maximizing their two norm contributions proves the formula. For an orthogonal
constant-cell projection $P_m$, Jensen gives
$\norm{(P_mh)_\pm}\le\norm{h_\pm}$. Combining these lower bounds with
the continuous $\norm h$ upper bound yields conservative support endpoints,
without restricting the unknown density to cells. If $U\ge S_\eta(h)$,
$L\ge S_\eta(-h)$ and the nuisance-field norm is at most $d$, the estimator
$w^\top y+(U-L)/2$ has bias at most $(U+L)/2+Rd$. The no-data interval
for our positive target is $[-\eta\norm\ell,R\norm\ell]$; both its center
and width replace the fitted interval on fallback. Projection error guards
are numerical checks, not validated floating-point bounds.

We retain all $R=1,2,3$, $\eta/R=0,0.1,0.25,0.5,1$ and cell sizes
24, 48, 96 on the saved 1,024-particle, 10\,\AA\ 10049 fit. Its unit-normalized
processed reference has negative-part norm 0.4579, so several stronger sign
constraints exclude that comparator; this is not evidence about the sign of
the underlying physical density. At $R=1,\eta=0.5,m=96$, the nominal support
half-width decreases from 0.1090 to 0.1061. The inherited one-degree nuisance
field bound remains 9.1621 per unit density norm. All pose-sensitive cases
still have zero sign power, including every class containing the reference.
This diagnoses this same-weight bound, not impossibility under sign information
or an experimentally calibrated density norm.

\input{cubic-pose-methods}

\subsection{A closer Fourier variational comparison}
We independently implement the fixed-pose Gaussian variational objective of
\citet{ullrich2020}, Equation~14, in a Hermitian Fourier grid with trilinear
slice interpolation. The original authors' full software and pose-learning
pipeline are not reproduced. CTFs, an independent pilot as prior mean, physical
target normalization and a declared prior-scale sweep are explicit extensions.
For $x\sim N(m_0,\tau^2I)$ and whitened $y=Ax+e$, put
$Q=A^\top A+\tau^{-2}I$. The diagonal-Gaussian optimum has the full posterior
mean and coordinate variances $1/Q_{jj}$. A target's full posterior variance
is $\ell^\top Q^{-1}\ell$, whereas its diagonal approximation is
$\sum_j\ell_j^2/Q_{jj}$. Differentiating the Gaussian objective verifies these
solutions without stochastic-training error. The identity
\[
 \norm{w}^2+\tau^2\norm{A^\top w-\ell}^2
   =\ell^\top Q^{-1}\ell,\qquad w=AQ^{-1}\ell,
\]
separately checks prior-predictive calibration.

Each stack uses 1,024 particles, radius 12 and two 10\,\AA\-sigma targets:
a central average and a contrast between centers at $z=\pm10$\,\AA.
The prior expected squared deviation norms are 0.25, 1 and 4; all settings
are retained. The sparse conditional calculations take 3.3--3.9 seconds per
stack and 45.0 MB per acquisition matrix. The full posterior's matched
prior-predictive coverage is 0.95, and the variance identity error is below
$4\times10^{-16}$. Diagonal feature intervals are \emph{wider} in every tested
case, by factors 1.073--1.415, with matched prior-predictive coverage
0.964--0.994. Diagonal covariance is therefore not a general explanation for
undercoverage of these targets.

Table~\ref{tab:fouriervi} and Figure~\ref{fig:fouriervi} instead report
fixed-map, known-noise coverage. Interpolation and finite-representation forward
discrepancy is 16.8\%, 16.2\% and 25.3\% across the three reference generators.
Together with prior shrinkage, this is a material baseline limitation. These
controls do not refute Bayesian prior-predictive guarantees or constitute
experimental density-coverage measurements. All matched-model and nonlinear
pose controls are retained in the public records.

We also audit each of these 18 estimators in the continuous cube without
changing its original affine center. Let $\kappa$ be the known difference
between its interpolated-prior center and the exact continuous-pilot center.
The fixed-pose bias bound is then $|\kappa|+2\norm{\ell-\A^*w}$. Audited
half-widths are 0.257--0.815 of no data and 56--352 times the original full
posterior widths. The nominal continuous-map checks are covered conservatively,
but sign power is numerically zero throughout, even after correcting
$\kappa$. Thus the broad continuous class already loses useful precision before
adding pose uncertainty. This does not establish impossibility for a physically
narrower class or a different estimator.

===== BEGIN FILE paper/two-pose-methods.tex =====
\subsection{Constructive ambiguity from two feasible pose designs}
Wide upper bounds alone cannot distinguish intrinsic ambiguity from a loose
audit. We therefore construct lower bounds from two allowed pose designs,
using the classical Gaussian testing argument \citep{donoho1994}. This is a
diagnostic on the same declared class, not a new minimax principle.

Let $A_0,A_1$ be two allowed observation operators, and let
$\rho_j$ belong to $\mathcal C=\{\rho:\norm{\rho-\rho_0^{\rm pilot}}\le B\}$.
Both designs have identity observation covariance. If
\begin{equation}
 D=\norm{A_1\rho_1-A_0\rho_0}<2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha),
 \label{eq:two-pose-distance}
\end{equation}
then every uniformly $1-\alpha$ valid interval whose length is deterministic
must have half-length at least
$|\langle\ell,\rho_1-\rho_0\rangle|/2$. Indeed, if a shorter interval
contained either feature with probability at least $1-\alpha$, its membership
test for one feature would distinguish the two hypotheses with both error
probabilities at most $\alpha$. The minimum sum of errors for their Gaussian
distributions is $2\Phi(-D/2)>2\alpha$, a contradiction. This conclusion does
not bound the expected length of arbitrary variable-length intervals.

Write $p=A_1\rho_0^{\rm pilot}-A_0\rho_0^{\rm pilot}$ and choose a distance
budget $\tau<2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$. For any observation weights $w$,
\begin{equation}
 G(w)=B\sum_{j=0}^1\norm{\ell-A_j^*w}-w^\top p+\tau\norm w
 \label{eq:two-pose-dual}
\end{equation}
upper-bounds the largest feasible feature gap for this fixed pair of pose
designs. To see this, insert $A_j^*w$ into the two feature pairings, apply
the density-ball bounds, and use
$w^\top(A_1\rho_1-A_0\rho_0)\le\tau\norm w$.

The same weights yield explicit continuous witnesses. Put
$h_j=\ell-A_j^*w$, choose $r_j\ge\norm{h_j}$, and set
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde\rho_1=\rho_0^{\rm pilot}+Bh_1/r_1,\qquad
 \widetilde\rho_0=\rho_0^{\rm pilot}-Bh_0/r_0.
\end{equation}
If $r_j=0$, its perturbation is set to zero. Their mean difference is
$p+\sum_j(B/r_j)(A_j\ell-A_jA_j^*w)$ and their feature difference is
$\sum_j(B/r_j)(\norm\ell^2-w^\top A_j\ell)$. Let $\overline D$ bound the
mean-distance norm. Multiplying both densities by
$\lambda=\min(1,\tau/\overline D)$ (one if $\overline D=0$) makes them feasible for
Equation~\eqref{eq:two-pose-distance}. This scaling preserves the original
class when $\norm{\rho_0^{\rm pilot}}\le B$, because zero is in the ball
and the ball is convex. Thus the scaled feature gap supplies a constructive
lower bound even if optimization is incomplete.

We minimize Equation~\eqref{eq:two-pose-dual} by iteratively reweighted
quadratic solves and retain both the best feasible pair and the best dual
weights, which may occur at different iterations. Continuous Gram integration
errors pad each residual norm and the mean-distance norm. Translation is a
real orthogonal rotation of each Fourier cosine/sine pair, so the phase-wrapped
Gram and target preserve those error norms. The witnesses are continuous
target/adjoint fields plus the known pilot; they are not restricted to a voxel
representation. Floating-point magnitude guards are additional numerical
checks, not validated interval arithmetic.

The prespecified development grid uses the existing 128-particle, radius-5
geometries and broad targets on three stacks. It includes identical nominal
poses, antipodal coherent rotations, and antipodal random joint-ball poses at
one and two degrees with $0.5\,\AA$ translation radius. The same random unit
vectors are used at both angular budgets. Independent conic programs check
small Hilbert-space cases; deliberately crude quadrature is checked against
the exact continuous sinc Gram; nonlinear constant-cell projections check
the phase convention. A serialization failure and the first complete grid
remain archived. The final rerun adds the numerical guards and separate
witness records requested by the focused mathematical audit.

\input{tables/two-pose-modulus}
The fixed-pair problems are solved to relative brackets below 0.5\%. Their
lower bounds remain substantially smaller than several pose-aware upper
intervals. This leaves a gap: the selected configurations need not maximize
ambiguity, so these results do not prove that the larger upper bounds can be
attained or substantially reduced. The testing statement also retains the
declared white-Gaussian noise, density and nuisance assumptions.

\paragraph{A bounded alternating ambiguity probe.}
We next test whether changing the selected poses strengthens a witness, using
one prespecified 10049 central-feature case at two degrees and $0.5\,\AA$.
Project the two unscaled continuous densities onto a nested constant-cell basis
containing the original pilot. Orthogonal projection cannot increase their
distance from that pilot, so they remain in the original continuous class.
We hold the projected densities fixed and minimize their whitened mean-image
distance over both allowed pose collections. Analytic cell Fourier moments
provide derivatives, while independent direct cell sums check every particle
at the saved feasible poses. A subsequent density step returns to the full
continuous modulus problem at those poses. Each witness is feasible without
a global pose-optimization claim.

The initial 24-, 48- and 72-cell pose steps give lower widths
0.09624, 0.12169 and 0.12438 of no data, all below the source continuous
witness's 0.12634. Cell projection changes the images and loses target energy;
these outcomes are retained. Once the mean distance falls below the testing
budget, pose fitting alone cannot enlarge that fixed pair's feature gap.
Refitting the continuous densities at the 72-cell step's poses raises the
lower width to 0.13884. The two further alternations allowed by the development
protocol raise it to 0.14594 and 0.14962, with final fixed-pair bracket gap
0.1422\%. We stop at the specified three rounds. This is a stronger selected
witness, not a global ambiguity limit. The
projected densities carry substantial negative-value energy (approximately
0.49 and 0.36 of total squared norm in the 72-cell pair), illustrating why
the stated signed class must not be confused with biological admissibility.
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/pose-adaptive-ambiguity-round01.pdf}
\caption{A continuous testing witness after the first alternating pose/density
refit on 10049, displayed as 48-cell averages of the two central slices.
The common color scale is symmetric and unclipped. These are constructed signed
densities in the declared mathematical class, not experimental reconstructions
or a pair asserted to be molecular structures. Their allowed poses and
whitened image-mean distance yield the conditional fixed-length lower bound;
the displayed projections are for visualization only.}
\label{fig:pose-adaptive-ambiguity}
\end{figure*}

===== BEGIN FILE paper/enclosing-domain.tex =====
\subsection{Fourier cancellation in the nonlinear remainder}
\label{app:enclosing-domain}
The higher-band failure motivates a further exploratory refinement of the
\emph{same} continuous-density class. The preceding frequency-wise Taylor
bound discards cancellation in the known adjoint field. For one particle let
\(f(x)=\operatorname{Re}\sum_q c_q\exp(2\pi i k_q^T x)\), where
\(c_q=(w_{Rq}+i w_{Iq})C_q/\sigma\). Let \(R=\sqrt{3}/2\), let \(a\) be
the rotation radius, and let \(s_i\) bound the norm of the three-dimensional
translation dual to the detector shift. For exact isometric detector
embeddings, \(s_i=s\); in computation we use the embedding pseudoinverse and
an explicit residual-phase correction, as recorded with the implementation.

For a joint scaled pose ball, the path \(y(t)=\exp(t\Omega)x+tb\),
\(0\leq t\leq1\), satisfies
\begin{equation}
 L=\sqrt{a^2R^2+s_i^2},\qquad H=a^2R,\qquad T=a^3R
\end{equation}
as bounds on its first, second and third derivative norms. An enclosing ball
has radius \(R+s_i\). An alternative enclosing coordinate cube has half-side
\begin{equation}
 r_i=\tfrac12+2R\sin\{\min(a,\pi)/2\}+s_i.
\end{equation}
Indeed, \(\norm{(\exp(t\Omega)-I)x}\leq
2R\sin\{\min(a,\pi)/2\}\), and translation adds at most \(s_i\).
This enlarges the integration domain of a \emph{known} field; it imposes no
new support or smoothness condition on the unknown density.

\begin{proposition}[Enclosing-domain remainder]
Let \(D_i\) contain every transformed unit cube along every allowed path,
and let \(S_m=\norm{D^m f}_{L^2(D_i),F}\) be the Frobenius derivative-tensor
norm. The second-order pose Taylor remainder has \(L^2\) norm at most
\begin{equation}
 r_{\mathrm{enc},i}=\tfrac16\{L^3 S_3+3LH S_2+T S_1\}.
 \label{eq:enclosing-remainder}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The third chain-rule derivative is the sum of the cubic derivative contraction,
three Hessian contractions with \(y'\) and \(y''\), and the gradient
contraction with \(y'''\). Cauchy--Schwarz bounds each contraction by its
Frobenius norm. The map from \(x\) to \(y(t)\) is rigid and has Jacobian one;
enlarging its image to \(D_i\) increases each nonnegative squared integral.
Minkowski's inequality and Taylor's integral remainder give
\eqref{eq:enclosing-remainder}.
\end{proof}

For either symmetric domain, write \(K_D(v)=\int_D e^{2\pi i v^Tx}\,dx\).
The exact real-arithmetic identity retaining cross-frequency terms is
\begin{align}
 S_m^2={}&\tfrac12(2\pi)^{2m}\operatorname{Re}
 \sum_{q,l}(k_q^Tk_l)^m\bigl[
 c_q\overline{c_l}K_D(k_q-k_l)\nonumber\\
 &\hspace{32mm}+(-1)^m c_qc_l K_D(k_q+k_l)\bigr].
\end{align}
The sum over ordered tensor derivatives yields \((k_q^Tk_l)^m\);
the sum-frequency sign is \(i^{2m}=(-1)^m\). For a ball of radius \(r\),
\(K_D(v)=4\pi r^3j_1(z)/z\), \(z=2\pi r\norm{v}\), with value
\(4\pi r^3/3\) at zero. For the coordinate cube,
\(K_D(v)=\prod_j 2r\operatorname{sinc}(2rv_j)\).
The scalar density bias receives \((B+P)\sum_i r_{\mathrm{enc},i}\).
Taking the smaller valid remainder for each particle is deterministic and
uses the original spectral event; no new random certificate is selected.
Magnitude-based roundoff guards remain heuristic, not validated arithmetic.

Independent spherical and tensor-product quadrature checks all ordered
derivative tensors through degree three. Direct nonlinear cube integration
also checks allowed joint poses and deliberately nonplanar frequency
embeddings. On the saved 1,024-particle higher-band example, the ball enclosure
reduces the cubic contribution from 56.493 to 32.623 after particle-wise
selection, still yielding no data. The subsequent expanded-cube probe reduces
it to 21.110, with total half-width 25.840, or 0.751 of no data. All particles
improve in that probe; its extra embedding-residual bias is below
\(5\times10^{-14}\). Both probes take approximately five CPU seconds and
retain the previous polynomial certificate and estimator weights. Nevertheless,
the three reference scenarios still have numerically zero feature-detection
power. This inexpensive refinement reduces a conservative remainder; it does
not solve the fine-feature usefulness or experimental calibration problem.

===== BEGIN FILE paper/cubic-pose-methods.tex =====
\subsection{Higher-order pose remainder diagnostic}\label{sec:cubicpose}
The enclosing-domain calculation extends to Taylor degree $d$. Let $S_j$ be
the $L^2$ Frobenius norm of the known Fourier adjoint field's $j$th derivative
tensor over the enclosing domain. For the rigid pose path
$y(t)=\exp(t\Omega)x+t b$, use
$M_1=\operatorname{hypot}(a\sqrt{3}/2,s_t\|B_{\rm det}\|)$ and
$M_j=a^j\sqrt{3}/2$ for $j\ge2$, where $B_{\rm det}$ maps detector shifts to
object coordinates. The joint pose ball justifies the hypotenuse expression.
The chain rule, tensor Cauchy--Schwarz and volume preservation give
\[
 \left\|(f\circ y)^{(d+1)}\right\|_{L^2}
 \le \sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\mathcal B_{d+1,j}(M_1,\ldots,M_{d+1})S_j,
\]
with partial exponential Bell polynomials $\mathcal B$. Division by $(d+1)!$
bounds the Taylor remainder. The existing approximate-embedding phase residual
also needs a higher-order Leibniz pad. These are standard differentiation and
norm inequalities, not a new general statistical theorem.

A declared two-case feasibility probe retains every degree in
Table~\ref{tab:higherremainder}, at identical weights, acquisition geometry and
one-degree/0.5\,\AA\ joint pose budgets. Both use EMPIAR-10049 geometry and the
same $B=2,P=1$ density class. The values include multiplication by $B+P$.
They show a potential reduction in one bias component. They are \emph{not}
confidence-interval widths: replacing a remainder while omitting the extra
polynomial fields would be invalid. The first feature's degree-two enclosing
remainder is 3.550 of its total bias bound 5.155; its sign power remains
negligible. No degree was selected by comparing resulting coverage.
The Gaussian sigmas are respectively 20 and 10\,\AA; both use frequency radius
12.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Remainder-only bounds at the same weights. Degree means retained Taylor
polynomial degree, not derivative order. No higher-order interval is inferred
from this table.}\label{tab:higherremainder}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Feature / particles & $d=2$ & $d=3$ & $d=4$ & $d=5$\\
\midrule
Pilot region, 128 & 3.550 & 0.815 & 0.160 & 0.027\\
Center, 1,024 & 21.110 & 5.694 & 1.287 & 0.250\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Analytic coefficient identities and independent nonlinear Taylor checks
support the implementation. Floating-point guards remain heuristic.

\paragraph{Full cubic extension.}
A separate bounded diagnostic retains all cubic fields for the first case;
its protocol and code precede its empirical outcome. Write the nonlinear phase
as $\Phi_0+t\Phi_1+t^2\Phi_2+t^3\Phi_3+\cdots$. The third exponential
coefficient is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_3&=i\Phi_3-\Phi_1\Phi_2-i\Phi_1^3/6,\\
 \Phi_3&=-a^2\|u_{\rm rot}\|^2\Phi_{1,\rm rot}/6.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last identity uses $[u]_\times^3=-\|u\|^2[u]_\times$; dropping it would
omit rotation curvature. For degree $m\in\{1,2,3\}$, the normalized symmetric
lift $z_\alpha=\sqrt{m!/\alpha!}\,u^\alpha$, $|\alpha|=m$, has
$\|z\|^2=\|u\|^{2m}\le1$. Thus there are $5+15+35=55$ columns per particle,
using twenty spatial monomials. Positive degree/particle scales $d_{im}$ give
a joint lifted radius $L=\sqrt{\sum_{im}d_{im}}$. Cheap quadrature chooses
these scales only; order-80 integration and a degree-six product-kernel pad
protect the continuous spectral audit. Four fresh Gaussian probes and forty
power steps use failure probability $10^{-6}/12$.

For the pilot-corrected estimator in Equation~\eqref{eq:estimator},
$\widehat\theta=\ip{\ell}{\rho_0}+w^\top(y-A_0\rho_0)$,
the residual cross-term argument remains valid with this larger field operator.
For $H\ge\|\ell-A_0^*w\|$, $c\ge\|F^*(\ell-A_0^*w)\|$,
$f\ge\sup_{\|v\|\le L}\|Fv\|$, $p\ge\|F^*\rho_0\|$ and quartic field
remainder $r$, the conditional bias bound is
\[
 B\sqrt{H^2+2Lc+f^2}+\min(Pf,Lp)+(B+P)r.
\]
Its proof expands the squared residual norm and applies Cauchy--Schwarz to the
known pilot. Twenty continuous cell and Gaussian moments evaluate the pairings.
Independent scalar phase recurrences, direct quadrature, adjoint identities and
the old quadratic restriction check signs and normalization. The quadratic and cubic intervals are alternatives; their unadjusted minimum
is not a joint confidence claim. The completed audit takes 2,187 seconds and 1.42 GB peak resident memory.
Its total bias bound is 2.467, comprising a 0.815 quartic remainder and
1.652 from the polynomial/density terms. Noise adds 0.601 to the half-width.
The relative width falls from 0.473 for the quadratic enclosing-domain audit
to 0.252, but minimum reference sign power is only
$1.48\times10^{-10}$. Thus retaining cubic terms improves the bound without
making this feature detectable under the assumed class. Merely removing the
remainder from the current expression would still leave a half-width above
the reference feature magnitude; that counterfactual is not a valid interval
or an impossibility result for a different estimator.

Follow-up numerical checks evaluate all 28,160 actual-frequency Gaussian moments
against independent order-200 quadrature (maximum per-column relative norm
error $2.35\times10^{-14}$), reproduce the fixed-pose residual bias, and verify
an actual-operator adjoint pairing. Selected continuous block-norm/design-scale
ratios are 0.982--1.029; no scale is changed after the probes. These checks do
not validate all floating-point errors. A stricter factor-twenty toy remainder
slack test fails at 35.57, which remains a conservatism finding; separate
nonlinear tests verify fourth-order error scaling. Neither these checks nor the
reduced interval calibrate experimental pose radii.

\paragraph{Pose-aware cubic weight design.}
The failed fixed-weight power result motivates optimizing the weights themselves.
A separate single-case development protocol, committed before fitting, retains
its target, class and pose budget, uses the inherited positive scales, and limits
L-BFGS-B to 30 iterations with a requested 40 evaluations. Every evaluation and
improving checkpoint is retained. Three approximate Ritz modes and a
log-sum-exp smoothing of 0.002 guide optimization. A fresh four-probe,
forty-step audit follows weight selection. Both design and final spectral audit
use order 64, while the nominal Gram uses order 80. The completed run takes
7,191 seconds and 2.59 GB peak memory. Its refined relative width is 0.180,
versus 0.252 without reoptimizing, but minimum reference sign power is only
0.00654. The optimizer reaches its 30-iteration limit; the audited triangle
objective is 2.322 with dual lower bound 0.139, a 0.940 relative gap. Thus this
run supplies neither a near-optimal weight design nor useful sign detection for
the original generator. The separately declared registered-generator result
and experimental application appear in Appendix~\ref{sec:referenceframe};
they retain these historical values and do not improve the weights.

Let $G=A_0A_0^*$, $a=A_0\ell$, and let $G_Q$ be its quadrature approximation.
If $E$ is the kernel-error bound and $t$ the transfer vector, set
$\eta=E\|t\|^2$ and
\[
 H(w)^2=\|\ell\|^2-2a^\top w+w^\top(G_Q+\eta I)w.
\]
The bound $|w^\top(G_Q-G)w|\le E(\sum_j|t_j|b_j(w))^2$
and Cauchy--Schwarz imply $G_Q+\eta I\succeq G$, where $b_j$ is the
real/imaginary pair amplitude. Hence $H$ is a convex affine-norm majorant of
the continuous residual. With nonnegative coefficient-mass matrix $M$ and
degree-six kernel pad $E_6$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 J(w)={}&BL\sqrt{\|F_Q(w)\|_{\rm op}^2+E_6\|Mb(w)\|^2}\\
       &+L\|F_{\rm cont}(w)^*\rho_0\|+(B+P)r_{\rm PSD}(w).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $r_{\rm PSD}$ is the Bell-weighted sum of real derivative-Gram norms,
with the approximate-embedding residual pad. Each term is convex and positively
homogeneous. Thus $z\|w\|+BH(w)+J(w)$ is a convex sum-width majorant.
The derivative-Gram diagonal safeguards and final cancellation guard remain
ordinary floating-point precautions, not validated numerical enclosures.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{proposition}[Continuous lower certificate for cubic design]
Suppose $g_J^\top w'\le J(w')$ for all $w'$, $\bar H\ge\|\ell-A_0^*w\|>0$,
and $e_G\ge\|(G_Q-G)w\|$. Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 f&=B/\bar H,\\
 d&=\|f(a-G_Qw)-g_J\|+fe_G,\\
 c&=\min(1,z/d).
\end{aligned}
\]
Then $\max\{0,cf(\|\ell\|^2-a^\top w)\}$ lower-bounds the infimum of the
sum-width majorant. Use $c=1$ if $d=0$.
\end{proposition}
\end{samepage}
\begin{proof}
Take $v=f(\ell-A_0^*w)$, so $\|v\|\le B$ and
$\|A_0(cv)-cg_J\|\le z$. Norm duality and the supporting inequality imply
$z\|w'\|+B\|\ell-A_0^*w'\|+J(w')\ge\ip{cv}{\ell}$ for every $w'$.
Replacing the continuous residual by its majorant preserves the lower bound.
The zero lower bound is also valid.
\end{proof}
The dual uses $a-G_Qw$, without $\eta w$, because its density direction is the
actual continuous residual. Any unit spatial directions supply spectral-norm
supports, including inaccurate or partial Ritz modes. Convex mixtures remain
supports; combining their gradient with the coefficient-mass gradient by the
normalized two-component norm inequality preserves this property even with
positive smoothing. Entropy means support equality at the candidate is not
asserted. A Ritz value is never used as an upper certificate. The reported gap
compares the unsmoothed, order-matched triangle objective; a later joint-cross
or folded-normal refinement does not inherit that gap.

An independently assembled four-coordinate conic problem gives optimum
2.071569215466, audited primal 2.071569215459 and continuous dual
2.071569195636. Their agreement is a numerical implementation check, not a
cryo-EM calibration result. The original conic test returned
\texttt{optimal\_inaccurate} at a provable zero-weight optimum; that failed
attempt is retained, and a separate analytic boundary check now covers it.
Directional gradients, convex supports and partial-mode bookkeeping are also
checked before the empirical fit.

A subsequent eight-coordinate, two-particle conic check uses unequal geometry
and nuisance budgets. SCS gives objective 1.998226582036, with an audited
relative gap $4.54\times10^{-7}$; a preceding CLARABEL failure on the same
geometry is retained. Random spatial-mode supports and empty-eigensolver failure
paths are checked separately. A fresh rerun of the zero-weight boundary gives
2.528968168770 versus analytic optimum 2.528968168766 while retaining the
\texttt{optimal\_inaccurate} warning. Final-weight checks tighten NUFFT
tolerance from $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-14}$: nominal Gram action changes by
$7.31\times10^{-13}$ relatively, and one cubic forward/adjoint pair by
$4.04\times10^{-13}$/$5.64\times10^{-13}$. The nominal quadratic change is
0.170 of the recorded roundoff guard. Fresh spectral upper/Ritz and
Rayleigh/Ritz ratios are 1.0903 and 0.99952. These empirical checks do not
validate all operator errors or remedy the optimization gap.

A separate block-plus-low-rank coordinate metric includes noise, nominal-density
and quartic-penalty curvature, while omitting the shared spectral and pilot
curvature. Its nonsymmetric forward map requires the transpose map for gradients.
A compute-only probe at the original weights verifies whitening to
$3.58\times10^{-13}$ relative error in 22.59 seconds; a small conic comparison
checks the resulting solver. These are numerical checks, not speedup or
usefulness findings. The original gap triggers a previously declared single
follow-up using the same starting weights and iteration budget. It completes
in 8,801 seconds at the thirty-iteration limit without convergence. Its
independently audited relative width is 0.223 and minimum reference sign power
is $7.73\times10^{-7}$, both worse than the original fit's 0.180 and 0.00654.
The relative surrogate gap is 0.977. All selected evaluations and checkpoints
are retained. A separately declared thirteen-dimensional convex design uses
the original fit in its span. The first restricted master meets its numerical
stopping threshold (guide gap $0.000365$) and selects the original weights,
with relative difference $4.61\times10^{-16}$. A fresh audit gives relative
width $0.179695$, minimum reference sign power $0.00663$ and full-space gap
$0.940164$. The small numerical metric changes do not reflect an improved
estimator. Total runtime is 1,934 seconds; the restricted guide does not certify
full-space convergence.


A subsequent adaptive enrichment grows this span from 13 to 19 columns.
Seven evaluations and five improving checkpoints complete in 3,477 seconds
at 2.76\,GB peak resident memory. Its audited relative width is 0.178365,
only 0.79\% smaller than the original 0.179785, and the full-space triangle
gap remains 0.927173. Original-/registered-frame minimum sign powers are
0.00817/0.96413 under supplied simulation noise. These are modest numerical
changes, not full-space convergence or experimental calibration.

\subsection{Joint density--pose trust-region development}
\label{sec:jointtrust}
The preceding designs optimize a triangle bound, even though final auditing
retains residual/pose cross terms. A new, separately declared design uses
\[
 J_{\rm joint}(w)=B\sup_{\|v\|\le L}\|h(w)-F(w)v\|.
\]
Here $h(w)=\ell-A_0^*w$. For fixed $v$, this is a norm of an affine function of $w$, so the supremum
is convex. It is no larger than $B(\|h(w)\|+L\|F(w)\|)$, with the same
enlarged pose ball and unchanged known-pilot, noise and quartic terms.
Robust least squares and trust-region methods are classical
\citep{elghaoui1997,adachi2017}; the following residual form supports the
continuous Fourier implementation, not a general optimization novelty claim.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{proposition}[Residual-controlled joint upper bound]
For fixed weights, suppose $\|h\|\le H$, $G=F_Q^*F_Q\succeq0$,
$\lambda_{\max}(G)\le U$, $\|G_{\rm cont}-G\|\le\epsilon_G$, and
$\|F_{\rm cont}^*h-b\|\le\epsilon_b$. For any $\lambda>U$ and any $x$, put
$D=\lambda I-G$ and $r=b-Dx$. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sup_{\|v\|\le L}\|h-F_{\rm cont}v\|^2
 &\le H^2+L^2\epsilon_G+2L\epsilon_b+\lambda L^2\\
 &\quad+2b^\top x-x^\top Dx+\frac{\|r\|^2}{\lambda-U}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{proposition}
\end{samepage}
\begin{proof}
The integration errors reduce the pose-dependent term to
$v^\top Gv-2b^\top v$. Completing the square bounds it by
$\lambda L^2+b^\top D^{-1}b$. The identity
$b^\top D^{-1}b=2b^\top x-x^\top Dx+r^\top D^{-1}r$ and
$D\succeq(\lambda-U)I$ give the result.
\end{proof}
Any reduced solve supplies $x$; its residual is charged explicitly. A Krylov
cache stores actual $GQ$ actions, without assuming an exact Lanczos recurrence.
All choices of $x,\lambda$ and the preceding joint upper bound are valid on
the same fixed-weight spectral event. Their minimum requires no extra failure
allowance; selecting new weights after seeing those probes would invalidate
that argument. Multiply the square root by $B$ and add the original known-
pilot and quartic terms. Real-arithmetic validity still does not enclose
floating-point/NUFFT error or calibrate experimental assumptions.

A reduced conic master accumulates feasible pose witnesses and rescores all
evaluated weights against the final cut set. Sampled target quadrature and
approximate separation guide selection only. A fresh final
spectral audit follows fixed weights. The independent robust-norm SDP check
gives 1.796133293662 versus guide 1.796133292859. Its first unscaled SCS
attempt reaches the solver limit; an equivalent unit-ball CLARABEL formulation
succeeds. Analytic hard-case and explicit-residual tests also pass after a
near-hard root-tolerance issue is corrected. These are small numerical checks.
Failed shifted solves retain the older valid upper bound. The declared empirical
fit completes in 2,321 seconds at 2.65\,GB peak memory. Two evaluations in the
unchanged thirteen-dimensional span select the second candidate. Its final-cut
restricted guide gap is $0.000885$, not a full-space convergence certificate.
The fresh audited half-width is 2.130112, or 0.175192 of no data, only 2.55\%
smaller than the original cubic design. The bias upper is 1.553146, compared
with 1.595052 for the preceding joint bound and 1.913367 for the triangle bound
at these same weights. The resolvent search reaches its declared lower
log-shift boundary without falling back; both evaluations are retained,
including the first master's \texttt{optimal\_inaccurate} status.
Minimum original-/registered-frame sign powers are 0.01433/0.97829. All six
conditional reference checks are retained without a tested coverage failure.
These results demonstrate a modest bound/design improvement, not calibrated
experimental inputs or full-space optimality. The real-image result below
still contains zero.
